title: why the world looks solid
hook: a rope on a dark path, and the snake that was never there

segments.voice: Yesterday, ahimsa, the courage not to strike. Your line was do no harm — start with your mouth. Did a sharp sentence go unsaid? Today we go back to the big ideas for a day. Day eighteen.
screen: `DO NO HARM — START WITH YOUR MOUTH.`

segments.voice: Dusk, on a path, and something is coiled across it. Your heart jumps before your mind has a word for it. Snake. You freeze. Your pulse is real. The fear is real. Then someone brings a lamp, and it's a rope. Just a rope, lying where it always was. Nothing about the rope changed. The snake was never there. And yet for a few seconds it ran your whole body. Teachers in this tradition tell that small story because it holds a very big word. A thing that is not what it seems, and works on you anyway.
screen: `SOMETHING COILED ON THE PATH.` → `THE FEAR IS REAL.` → `A LAMP. A ROPE.`

segments.voice: Maya. It often gets translated as illusion, and that one word causes a lot of confusion. It sounds like the tradition is saying the world is fake. Your kitchen, your friends, your job, none of it real. That isn't what it says. The Svetasvatara Upanishad puts it this way: know that nature is maya, and that the great Lord is the one who works the maya. So maya isn't nothing. It's the power that makes the world appear the way it does, so convincingly that we stop looking past it. Schools of the tradition read this differently, and they've argued about it with great care. Advaita Vedanta, the school of Shankara, says the world we see is an appearance laid over Brahman, the way the snake is laid over the rope. The rope is what's really there. Other schools, like those of Ramanuja and Madhva, hold that the world is fully real, made by God, and that maya names God's wondrous power. Both readings agree on one thing. The surface is not the whole story. And that's where the word walks into an ordinary day. A post makes someone's life look perfect. A comment feels like an attack on all of you. A bad morning looks like a bad life. Each one is a snake on the path, until the lamp comes. Neither reading asks anyone to stop living in the world. Only to stop gripping it as if the surface were everything. Hold it lightly.
screen: `NOT FAKE. NOT THE WHOLE STORY.` · `THE POWER THAT MAKES IT APPEAR.` · `SNAKE ON A ROPE, OR GOD'S POWER?` · `A POST. A COMMENT. A BAD MORNING.` · then, large: `HOLD IT LIGHTLY.`

segments.voice: Today's practice: bring the lamp. Breathe once, slowly. Recall one thing this week that made your heart jump. A message, a look, a number, a picture of someone else's life. Feel the jump again, just a little. Don't push it away. Now look at it again, slowly, as if someone had brought a lamp. What is actually there? Let the tightness loosen as much as it wants to. The bell holds the time.
Maya. The power that makes the world appear, so well that we stop looking past the surface. The snake that turns out to be rope. Eighteenth word.
Your line: hold it lightly. Today, when something makes you jump, take one breath and ask: snake, or rope? Day eighteen.

howItsDone: Hindu teachers explain maya through stories like the rope and the snake, and the schools of Vedanta read it in different ways, some as the appearance of the world over Brahman, others as God's real and wondrous power.

original.note: Sanskrit: the power that makes things appear; often translated as illusion.

trapdoor: what you thought: maya means everything is an illusion.
what it means: the power that makes the world appear, so well we stop looking past the surface. hold it lightly.
what a scholar hears: Svetasvatara Upanishad 4.10, nature as maya and the Lord as its maker; Advaita reads it as appearance over Brahman, Vishishtadvaita and Dvaita as God's real power.

notes: Svetasvatara Upanishad 4.10 paraphrased ('know that nature is maya, and the great Lord the maker of maya'). Max Müller 1884 (SBE 15) has a translation; not quoted because exact wording unverified. Confirm verse number and paraphrase.

School summaries: Advaita (Shankara) world as appearance (vivarta) over Brahman; Vishishtadvaita (Ramanuja) and Dvaita (Madhva) hold the world real, with maya understood as God's wondrous power. Confirm these are fair and brief enough, with no ranking.
'Teachers have told that small story for centuries': the rope-snake analogy appears in Shankara's commentaries and later Advaita texts; 'for centuries' left vague on purpose. Confirm.
